{"id": "7:169/q29", "question": "What wider recitation and textual observations occur in the notes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:169/q29/p1", "position": "Reading transmission depends on trusted authorities and mastered routes.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī gives biographies and reliability assessments for ʿAbd al-Wāḥid, Ibn Mujāhid, al-Sāmirī, Ṣāliḥ, Ibn Shanabūdh and Qāḍī Abū Faraj, including late memory criticism of al-Sāmirī. Ibn Mujāhid lived 245–324 AH and first canonized seven readings, with 300 senior pupils and 84 deputies; al-Sāmirī lived about 295–386 and weakened late; Ibn Shanabūdh died 328 and admitted sound readings beyond the written muṣḥaf; ʿAbd al-Wāḥid died 349, Ṣāliḥ about 380, and Qāḍī Abū Faraj at 85 in 390."}, {"id": "7:169/q29/p2", "position": "Licensed readings may be combined only after separate mastery.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī and al-Suyūṭī say one may use a licensed variant without reciting all forms, and combined recitation follows separate mastery. They report differing full-cycle requirements, Egyptian word-by-word and Syrian pause methods, and avoidance of mixed routes. Al-Kamāl al-Ḍarīr studied nineteen full cycles; Ibn al-Jazarī reports twenty-one required by his teachers and another forty-cycle precedent. Some allow one cycle per reader but separate Nāfiʿ and Ḥamza transmitters; mastery and authorization remove later separate-cycle requirements."}, {"id": "7:169/q29/p3", "position": "Nearby readings and assimilation rules are also noted.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid reports Abū ʿAmr’s doubled يمسكون and ولا تمسكوا; al-Naḥḥās says rāʾ cannot assimilate into lām because of vibration, citing 83:14."}, {"id": "7:169/q29/p4", "position": "Verse endings and pauses are established through transmitted practice.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī cites Umm Salama’s verse-by-verse recitation, distinguishes consistent from occasional stops and analogical verse boundaries, and compares endings to prose rhyme and rajaz."}, {"id": "7:169/q29/p5", "position": "Retained ghunna in assimilation is disputed between incomplete assimilation and concealment.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī prefers incomplete assimilation with retained ghunna because audible shadda remains; al-Sakhāwī calls it concealment, while Abū ʿAmr defines complete assimilation by no residual trace."}, {"id": "7:169/q29/p6", "position": "Sūra transitions have rules for tahlīl, takbīr and basmala.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī retains original vowels at sūra transitions, allows devotional tahlīl lengthening, and distinguishes takbīr attached to the end from that at the beginning, including prostration and prayer."}, {"id": "7:169/q29/p7", "position": "Verse order comes through prophetic instruction; sūra order is discussed.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī cites Makkī, al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr, Mālik and al-Baghawī for prophetic instruction in verse arrangement; Ibn Ḥajar’s inferred companion discretion is answered by other reports. Al-Tawba lacks an opening basmala in Makkī’s account because no instruction placed one; al-Baghawī distinguishes revelation order from recitation order."}]}
{"id": "7:169/q30", "question": "Can modern scientific meanings be read into the Quran without linguistic evidence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:169/q30/p1", "position": "Such projections lack linguistic and transmitted support.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects projecting atoms, spacecraft, gravity, Earth’s rotation or engineering onto the Quran; she says no sound Prophetic report taught these interpretations and stresses Arabic expression."}]}
{"id": "7:170/q01", "question": "Who are those who hold fast to the Book?", "turns_on": "Whether the contextual Israelites are all scriptural adherents, only believers who accepted Muḥammad, or an example of a general class; some identify the addressees as Muslims.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q01/p1", "position": "Believers among the People of the Book, especially ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan specifies believers of earlier communities (IBNABIHATIM, DURR); the majority of exegetes say believing People of the Book (WAHIDI-BASIT). Mujāhid's reports name Ibn Salām and companions, who neither distorted or concealed Moses' Book nor profited from it (BAGHAWI, BURSEVI, ALUSI); IBNJAWZI says the verse was revealed about them, and MUQATIL reports the same. IBNASHUR identifies Jews who awaited and accepted the foretold final messenger; ISLAHI calls them a small truth-preserving group who later converted."}, {"id": "7:170/q01/p2", "position": "Jews and Christians who adhere to scripture.", "reasons": "MUJAHID says Jews and Christians; TAB-FULL reports his identification as possible, and THALABI specifies preserving Moses' scripture without concealment or violating lawful and forbidden rulings. DURR reports that he meant some of them."}, {"id": "7:170/q01/p3", "position": "Muḥammad's community, with Muḥammad himself among them.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ reports this from Ibn ʿAbbās (WAHIDI-BASIT); THALABI says Muḥammad is among them. IBNASHUR also allows an address to Muslims, assuring them they will not treat their Book as the Jews treated theirs."}, {"id": "7:170/q01/p4", "position": "Jews who faithfully observe the Torah and their own religious duties.", "reasons": "QURTUBI and the Şevkânî report identify Torah-observant Jews; KURANYOLU prefers this contextual reading of prayer, citing prayer in all revealed religions via Rāghib. STUDYQURAN says Jews following Torah and Mosaic law receive reward, comparing 2:62 and 5:69."}, {"id": "7:170/q01/p5", "position": "Anyone who fulfills the verse's conditions, though Israelites are the immediate setting.", "reasons": "TABATABAI calls the wording general and independent despite its Israelite setting; KURANYOLU says the promise applies beyond Jews to everyone fulfilling its condition."}]}
{"id": "7:170/q02", "question": "How is يُمَسِّكُونَ read?", "turns_on": "The reported recitations differ in verb stem, consonant doubling and tense; arguments invoke Arabic government by bi, parallel Qurʾānic forms, the force of intensification, and agreement with aqāmū.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q02/p1", "position": "The common reading is yumassikūn, with open mīm and doubled sīn.", "reasons": "TAB-FULL derives it from massaka; IBNMUJAHID names Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim; Abū ʿAmr also uses it and alone doubles the related verb in 60:10. FĀRISĪ, WAHIDI-BASIT, RAZI and QURTUBI prefer its force of whole, persistent or repeated adherence; FĀRISĪ compares 3:119 and 4:150, QURTUBI cites Kaʿb's covenant-and-sieve poem. Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim favor the bi construction and Ubayy's past variant; WAHIDI notes the common direct-object idiom amsaktuhu. IBNKHALAWAYH calls it renewed adherence; QIRAAT-ER contrasts intensive Form II with simple Form IV. IBNATIYYA, TABRISI and ABUHAYYAN say both have the same basic sense."}, {"id": "7:170/q02/p2", "position": "The light reading is yumsikūn, with still mīm and undoubled sīn, from amsaka.", "reasons": "Reported for ʿUmar, Abū al-ʿĀliya, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, and in NASHR for Abū Jaʿfar; ALUSI also names Ḥammād, while SAMIN reports Abū ʿAmr. IBNMUJAHID says Abū Bakr also lightens 60:10, unlike Abū ʿAmr. IBNKHALAWAYH cites 33:37; FĀRISĪ and WAHIDI cite 2:229, 33:37 and 5:4 for related forms. NAHHAS cites ordinary Arabic and 60:10; QIRAAT-ER calls Form IV simple retention. FĀRISĪ accepts light 60:10 for retaining a wife and says Forms IV and II may coincide."}, {"id": "7:170/q02/p3", "position": "A variant uses the past tense istamsakū, 'held fast.'", "reasons": "Reported for al-Aʿmash; ABUHAYYAN also attributes it to ʿAbd Allāh, and ALUSI names Ibn Masʿūd. Some reports give the fuller wa-lladhīna istamsakū bi-l-kitāb."}, {"id": "7:170/q02/p4", "position": "Ubayy's variant uses a past verb, reported as masakū or tamassakū.", "reasons": "THALABI and BAGHAWI say its tense matches aqāmū; reports vary between masakū, musikū, and tamassakū bi-l-kitāb. IBNKHALAWAYH says Ubayy's form is related to the doubled reading; JISHUMI's wording is tamassakū bi-l-qirāʾa."}]}
{"id": "7:170/q03", "question": "What does holding fast to the Book require?", "turns_on": "Whether the action is described as observance of the present scripture alone or as including acceptance of a later revelation it foretells.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q03/p1", "position": "It means believing scripture, acting by its commands, avoiding its prohibitions, and judging by it.", "reasons": "MUQATIL adds no distortion or legalizing forbidden things; TAB-FULL includes acting within God's bounds. FARRĀʾ says taking what the Book contains, ZAJJAJ says belief and judgment, and IBNKATHIR says scripture leads to Muḥammad because it foretells him. BAGHAWI, THALABI, QURTUBI, STUDYQURAN and others stress observance. WAHIDI-BASIT reports an image of clutching what promises deliverance; BIQAI stresses continuous firm adherence amid corruption and refraining from false claims about God."}, {"id": "7:170/q03/p2", "position": "True adherence to an earlier Book includes following its abrogating successor.", "reasons": "BIQAI says the earlier revelation itself witnesses to its successor, so clinging to it requires leaving it when abrogated."}]}
{"id": "7:170/q04", "question": "Which Book is meant by ٱلْكِتَٰبِ?", "turns_on": "Whether the definite Book continues the reference to Israel's inherited scripture in 7:169 or names scripture more broadly; identifying the adherents as Muḥammad's community yields the Qurʾān.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q04/p1", "position": "The Torah, the Book given to Moses or inherited by Israel.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd identifies Moses' Book in TAB-FULL, IBNABIHATIM and DURR. Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd describe its preservation without alteration or concealment in TABRISI. WAHIDI-BASIT calls this the majority view; ABUHAYYAN prefers the same scripture as 7:169. TABATABAI says Torah in the Israelite setting, though also allo

BURSEVI and ALUSI pair the same two identifications."}, {"id": "7:170/q04/p3", "position": "All divine books.", "reasons": "ABUHAYYAN reports this alternative to the contextually inherited scripture."}, {"id": "7:170/q04/p4", "position": "The Torah together with the Gospel.", "reasons": "TABATABAI offers this as another way to understand the Book in the Israelite setting."}]}
{"id": "7:170/q05", "question": "How do the verb forms and بِ work in يُمَسِّكُونَ بِٱلْكِتَٰبِ?", "turns_on": "Whether the chosen stem directly takes bi or has an understood object; several sources also treat the stems as equivalent in basic sense.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q05/p1", "position": "The doubled form functions like tamassaka, taking bi as the instrument of adherence.", "reasons": "BAGHAWI, IBNATIYYA and Abu Ubayd with Abu Hatim contrast masaktu bi-shayʾ with direct-object amsaktuhu. ABUHAYYAN and SAMIN explain that faʿʿala may have tafaʿʿala's sense; Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr's covenant-and-sieve couplet is cited by NAHHAS, IBNATIYYA, SAMIN and QURTUBI. IBNJAWZI reports Ibn al-Anbārī's related Arabic forms."}, {"id": "7:170/q05/p2", "position": "On the light form, amsaka has an omitted object, while bi marks circumstance or instrument.", "reasons": "ABUHAYYAN supplies their deeds as object and cites transitive usage at 22:65. SAMIN supplies their religion and deeds, with the Book's commands and prohibitions as instrument."}, {"id": "7:170/q05/p3", "position": "Amsaka, masaka, tamassaka and istamsaka are equivalent Arabic ways to say 'hold fast.'", "reasons": "WAHIDI-BASIT, IBNATIYYA, TABRISI, RAZI, NASAFI, ALUSI and TABATABAI report this lexical equivalence; FĀRISĪ says Form IV and II can coincide in meaning. Kaʿb's poem illustrates more than one form."}]}
{"id": "7:170/q06", "question": "How is وَٱلَّذِينَ joined to the preceding verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the wāw begins a fresh promise or coordinates with alladhīna yattaqūn in the preceding verse; the latter changes the status of the promise to a separate reinforcing statement.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q06/p1", "position": "It begins a new nominative clause whose promise is its predicate.", "reasons": "ZAJJAJ states alladhīna is nominative; NAHHAS, most grammarians in WAHIDI-BASIT, RAZI, NASAFI, TABRISI and SAMIN take it as topic. ABUHAYYAN and SAMIN prefer this apparent syntax; RAZI says a warning followed by promise parallels 18:30."}, {"id": "7:170/q06/p2", "position": "It is genitive, coordinated with 'those who fear' in 7:169; the Hereafter is better for both.", "reasons": "IBNATIYYA, BURSEVI and the grammarians reported by WAHIDI-BASIT give the connection; RAZI and NASAFI say the following promise reinforces it. BAYDAWI, ALUSI, ABUHAYYAN and SAMIN report it; SAMIN quotes Zamakhsharī's view that the promise is parenthetical, but objects that 'independent' is the precise term because it does not interrupt syntactically connected elements."}]}
{"id": "7:170/q07", "question": "On the new-clause reading, how is its predicate linked to 'those who hold fast'?", "turns_on": "Whether the return to the nominative subject is implicit, expressed through the generic or overt noun, carried by the article, or supplied by an omitted predicate.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q07/p1", "position": "The predicate is the promise with an understood minhum, 'the reformers among them.'", "reasons": "ZAJJAJ prefers this because unbelievers' good acts are lost, citing 47:1 and 88:2–4; believers fulfill faith and duties. NAHHAS, TABRISI, Ibn al-Anbārī in IBNJAWZI, WAHIDI-BASIT and most Basrans in SAMIN and ALUSI supply the return; Ibn al-Anbārī notes some addressees did not reform, denying prophets and Muhammad's foretold coming."}, {"id": "7:170/q07/p2", "position": "The overt phrase 'the reformers' replaces or semantically repeats a pronoun referring to those people.", "reasons": "ZAJJAJ reports a semantic-antecedent argument, illustrated by believer/one who fears God rather than a mere alternative name such as Zayd/Abū ʿAmr. WAHIDI-BASIT and IBNJAWZI cite usage and poetry for making an implied pronoun overt; WAHIDI reports Abū Bakr's preference for the first of two analyses. TABRISI says 'their reward' is the intended sense; ITQAN gives this as manifest noun replacing pronoun. SAMIN attributes semantic repetition to al-Akhfash, citing nominal and relative-clause analogies; ABUHAYYAN reports Abū al-Baqāʾ's acceptance."}, {"id": "7:170/q07/p3", "position": "The general class 'reformers' includes those holding fast and thus itself links the clauses.", "reasons": "ABUHAYYAN prefers no deletion; SAMIN attributes this to Abū al-Baqāʾ, accepts it, and adduces ala layta shiʿrī and niʿma al-rajulu Zayd. IBNASHUR says the description already marks them as reformers and omission gives concise praise."}, {"id": "7:170/q07/p4", "position": "The definite article in al-muṣliḥīn stands for a possessive pronoun, meaning 'their reformers.'", "reasons": "SAMIN gives the Kufan explanation and comparisons from 79:41, 38:50 and 30:3; ALUSI lists it among the predicate links."}, {"id": "7:170/q07/p5", "position": "The subject has an omitted predicate such as 'We reward them,' and the promise explains or confirms it.", "reasons": "WAHIDI-BASIT reports grammarians inferring 'We give them their reward' from the causal force of the next sentence; TABRISI similarly says the cause stands for the result. Al-Ḥawfī and Abū al-Baqāʾ supply a link, but ABUHAYYAN and SAMIN object that deletion is unnecessary."}]}
{"id": "7:170/q08", "question": "Why is prayer expressed by the past verb أَقَامُوا after a present verb?", "turns_on": "Whether the differing tenses signal timing or theological context, or are resolved by interpreted coordination; Ubayy's variant removes the mismatch.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q08/p1", "position": "The past has a future or conditional force in context, so tense coordination is valid.", "reasons": "BURHAN reports Ibn ʿUmarūn and others requiring coordinated verbs to match tense but allowing interpreted shifts where meaning remains clear; it compares 25:66 and 25:75."}, {"id": "7:170/q08/p2", "position": "The past prevents an earlier community from using its former prayer to justify remaining in its old religion.", "reasons": "BIQAI ties the wording to the obligation to accept a successor revelation."}, {"id": "7:170/q08/p3", "position": "The present marks continuous adherence, while prayer takes place at appointed times.", "reasons": "ALUSI contrasts the well-known verb's ongoing force with prayer's prescribed timing; BAYDAWI says prayer's distinct singular verb signals its superiority among adherent acts."}, {"id": "7:170/q08/p4", "position": "A past-tense reading of 'held fast' gives direct tense agreement with 'established.'", "reasons": "THALABI praises Ubayy's reading and BAGHAWI says a past verb rarely coordinates with a present except by meaning."}]}
{"id": "7:170/q09", "question": "What does establishing prayer mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether ṣalāh marks specifically the Islamic prayer and acceptance of Muḥammad or prayer as observed under an earlier revealed religion.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q09/p1", "position": "Perform prayer faithfully, especially at its proper time and within its prescribed bounds.", "reasons": "Al-Zuhrī specifies proper time in IBNABIHATIM; TAB-FULL says do not neglect its times or boundaries. MUQATIL and THALABI include establishment in observance of scripture."}, {"id": "7:170/q09/p2", "position": "It is the prayer prescribed by Muḥammad, a sign of accepting him and Islam.", "reasons": "WAHIDI-WAJIZ specifies Muḥammad's prayer. IBNASHUR treats prayer as a metonym for accepting Muḥammad, since Islam is marked by prayer and Muslims are people of the qibla; KURANYOLU reports his suggestion of Jews recognizing Jesus but rejecting distorted Christianity before believing Muḥammad, or of Muslims."}, {"id": "7:170/q09/p3", "position": "It means prayer or ritual in the Jews' own religion.", "reasons": "KURANYOLU prefers its lexical sense in context; it cites Rāghib's observation that prayer exists in every revealed religion though practices differ, supporting a Jewish referent."}]}
{"id": "7:170/q10", "question": "Why is prayer singled out after holding fast to the Book?", "turns_on": "The notes give complementary emphases: prayer's rank among scriptural duties, a prior history of neglect, and its role as a visible sign of covenantal fidelity.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q10/p1", "position": "Prayer is included in scripture's commands but mentioned separately for its exceptional rank.", "reasons": "WAHIDI-BASIT and TABRISI stress its high rank or obligation; QUSHAYRI, RAZI and BURSEVI call it the greatest worship after faith or knowledge of God. NASAFI, ABUHAYYAN, BURHAN, ITQAN, ALUSI and TABATABAI call it religion's pillar; ABUHAYYAN adds the boundary from shirk, TABATABAI remembrance of God and submission. BURSEVI's Persian couplet pictures it supporting religion's house. ITQAN explains the general-to-specific device, comparing prayer, Gabriel and Michael at 4:103, 2:98 and 3:104; BURHAN calls it tajrīd and cites Ibn Mālik's requirements of wāw and a distinguishing merit. BURHAN also reports a dispute whether the preceding general expression includes or excludes the special item, with a poetry analogy and 26:148, where both readings are possible because 'gardens' is indefinite."}, {"id": "7:170/q10/p2", "position": "Prayer is emphasized because earlier people had abandoned it.", "reasons": "BIQAI cites 19:59 and also calls prayer one of religion's greatest rites."}, {"id": "7:170/q10/p3", "position": "Persevering in prayer manifests adherence to scripture and guards God's covenant.", "reasons": "ISLAHI uses it to characterize the small group that prese

{"id": "7:170/q11", "question": "Whose reward does God promise not to waste, and what is promised?", "turns_on": "Whether the promise is restricted to faithful reformers among the addressed group or stated as a rule for every reformer; the notes also differ in how they describe reform.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q11/p1", "position": "The reformers among the believers who hold the Book receive the reward of their faithful deeds.", "reasons": "ZAJJAJ limits it to believers because disbelievers' works are lost, citing 47:1 and 88:2–4; he compares 18:30 and requires belief, duties, and practice. IBNABIHATIM reports al-Ḥasan's 'believers among them.' Ibn al-Anbārī says some of the group failed to reform, by disobeying, denying prophets, or rejecting Muhammad's foretold coming. IBNKATHIR and ELMALILI identify adherents who establish prayer as reformers."}, {"id": "7:170/q11/p2", "position": "The promise covers all reformers who fulfill its condition and assures full recompense.", "reasons": "TABRISI says each receives what work deserves. BIQAI says no recompense is lost in any way; BURSEVI and al-Kāshifī say their words and deeds are fully paid. STUDYQURAN compares 3:171, 9:120, 11:115, 12:56, 12:90 and 18:30; it also cites 2:62 and 5:69 for Jews, Sabeans and Christians who believe and act well. KURANYOLU says the general wording extends beyond Jews, rejects condemnation of an entire people as unjust, and compares Israel's conditional mercy at 17:4–8. SAMARRAI says the subgroup falls in the wider class of reformers."}, {"id": "7:170/q11/p3", "position": "Reform involves outward obedience and inward purification, by which the self becomes receptive to divine light.", "reasons": "BURSEVI says the self must be disciplined; TABATABAI links adherence to scripture with reform of human nature and social life, citing 30:30 and 3:19, and rejects the claim that divine law does not serve human welfare."}]}
{"id": "7:170/q12", "question": "Why say 'the reward of the reformers' rather than 'their reward'?", "turns_on": "The stated effects of the overt noun are inclusion of a wider class, naming reform as the cause of reward, and stylistic explicitness.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q12/p1", "position": "The explicit class name identifies the adherents as reformers and extends the promise to every reformer.", "reasons": "SAMARRAI-ASRAR and both SAMARRAI-LAMASAT notes say the named subgroup belongs to the general class; BIQAI likewise says the reward is generalized. IBNASHUR sees concise praise because the earlier description already entails reform."}, {"id": "7:170/q12/p2", "position": "The explicit noun makes reform the stated reason they are saved or rewarded.", "reasons": "BURHAN says the noun in place of a pronoun gives this cause; ALUSI includes the same implication in the analysis of the overt noun."}, {"id": "7:170/q12/p3", "position": "The verse uses a manifest synonym instead of repeating a pronoun or exact wording.", "reasons": "ITQAN says this is more eloquent than exact repetition and compares the reformers' reward here to the reward of one who does good in Hūd 11:115; it also notes a parallel manifest noun in al-Kahf."}]}
{"id": "7:170/q13", "question": "How does this verse relate to the surrounding account?", "turns_on": "The notes connect the verse to the preceding corruption, the covenant setting, or the earlier mountain episode.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q13/p1", "position": "It contrasts corrupt Israelites with faithful reformers who preserve scripture and receive reward.", "reasons": "BIQAI opposes them to those who falsely spoke about God and spoiled the Book, linking the faithful to 7:159. IBNASHUR says covenant-breakers are followed by those upholding scripture and its prophetic message; KURANYOLU contrasts greed and abandoned commands in 7:169 with those who remain faithful. STUDYQURAN says the larger discussion returns to Israel's later disobedience and punishments. KURANYOLU says 7:168–170 confirms justice for Jews and others and rejects collective condemnation, citing 17:4–8."}, {"id": "7:170/q13/p2", "position": "It recalls the covenant and divine promise; the following reminder addresses both Israel's covenant and humanity's primordial covenant.", "reasons": "QUSHAYRI emphasizes God's true promise and loving care in making servants know Him. ELMALILI identifies the two covenants in the next reminder."}, {"id": "7:170/q13/p3", "position": "The preceding mountain-lifting episode means God raised the mountain above them.", "reasons": "MAJAZ explains nataqnā al-jabal through lines by al-ʿAjjāj and Ruʾba using nataqa for lifting or raising; QUSHAYRI says coerced assent to the Book was soon answered with distortion."}]}
{"id": "7:170/q14", "question": "What inward meanings are drawn from holding the Book, prayer and God's promise?", "turns_on": "These are complementary inward readings of adherence, worship, reward and divine address.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q14/p1", "position": "Holding the Book is faith and a means of eventual safety; prayer is excellence and present communion, leading to divine pleasure.", "reasons": "QUSHAYRI pairs faith with immediate safety and excellence with deferred pleasure, then pairs adherence with final salvation and prayer with present intimate communion."}, {"id": "7:170/q14/p2", "position": "Hope in God's generosity is never wasted and brings blessing, favor, honor and support.", "reasons": "QUSHAYRI says the hopeful bargain does not fail; a step toward God's door brings blessing in the next life, lifted aspirations win present favor, and reliance on His generosity brings honor in both worlds and sufficiency."}, {"id": "7:170/q14/p3", "position": "Voluntary loving obedience differs from coerced compliance, which does not recognize God's worth.", "reasons": "QUSHAYRI cites poems questioning affection requiring an advocate and comparing admonition of a fickle person to writing on water; forced affection is unnatural. Those coerced to accept the Book soon distorted it."}, {"id": "7:170/q14/p4", "position": "God's prior care gives gnosis before created influence, while one address yields differing inward responses.", "reasons": "QUSHAYRI says gnosis precedes what others see, effects in hearts, and speech of kin; a poem depicts divine love finding the heart ready before it knows love. Some recognize God through a near address, others remain veiled; some affirm unity when unveiled, others deny despite witnessing."}]}
{"id": "7:170/q15", "question": "What accounts illustrate the danger of later neglecting scripture and inward reform?", "turns_on": "The reported examples differ in speaker and event but illustrate the same later spiritual decline.", "positions": [{"id": "7:170/q15/p1", "position": "Later people may abandon the Qurʾān for worldly adornment and need spiritual discipline to overcome doubt.", "reasons": "BURSEVI contrasts blessed predecessors with wretched successors and says only divine enabling and a skilled spiritual guide can train the self and remove doubt. An unattributed Persian couplet depicts living as though in a grave without concern for death or winter provision."}, {"id": "7:170/q15/p2", "position": "Al-Ḥasan recalled seventy Badr veterans whose asceticism and joy in hardship surpassed later people.", "reasons": "He says they abstained from lawful things more than later people avoid unlawful ones, seemed mad to later observers, and feared lawful wealth would corrupt their hearts."}, {"id": "7:170/q15/p3", "position": "Uways told Hurm that doubt had entered hearts so deeply that admonition no longer helped.", "reasons": "BURSEVI reports their conversation about where to live and Syria's livelihood."}]}

{"id": "7:180/q04", "question": "Why are the names called most beautiful, and which qualify?", "turns_on": "Whether all fitting names or especially appealing mercy names are intended, and whether beauty lies in meaning or authorization.", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q04/p1", "position": "All God's names are beautiful because they convey true perfection, praise or freedom from defect.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās affirms all names; examples include Raḥmān, Raḥīm, Malik, Quddūs, Salām, ʿAzīz and Jabbār. {"id": "7:180/q06", "question": "How is the hamza of al-asmāʾ treated at pause?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q06/p1", "position": "At pause on al-asmāʾ al-ḥusnā, Ḥamza has naql or sakt combined with five final-hamza treatments.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī counts ten transmitted routes and rejects unsupported full realization without sakt; predecessors agree on naql at pause."}]}

{"id": "7:180/q08", "question": "What does enumerating the ninety-nine names entail?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q08/p1", "position": "It entails counting and memorizing them, believing and revering them, and reflecting on their meanings.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds aspiring through the names; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says faith in all their meanings; Kuran Yolu adds internalizing their beliefs."}]}
{"id": "7:180/q09", "question": "What is the status of the detailed ninety-nine-name lists?", "turns_on": "Whether the itemized lists are part of the sound core saying and whether every entry occurs in the Qurʾan.", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q09/p1", "position": "The core promise is sound; the Tirmidhī itemized list is solitary, anomalous in entries, and may be a narrator's insertion.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the list non-mutawātir; al-Tirmidhī calls it gharīb through trustworthy Ṣafwān. {"id": "7:180/q10", "question": "How are the divine names classified?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q10/p1", "position": "They divide into essential, active and negative attributes.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī, al-Rāzī, the Najmiyya and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī give these kinds; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes nonrelational self-attributes, self-attributes with relations, and purely relational terms. {"id": "7:180/q11", "question": "Which is the Greatest Name, and what makes it greatest?", "turns_on": "Whether it is Allah as an all-comprehensive designation, a real divine manifestation, or an effective verbal formula.", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q11/p1", "position": "Allah is the all-encompassing essence-name and is often called the Greatest Name.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī locates the Greatest Name in the essence-name; al-Bursawī says Allah comprehends all perfections. Ibn al-ʿArabī restricts prayer formulas to Qurʾan and five canonical hadith books including the Muwaṭṭaʾ. Al-Ālūsī allows carefully vetted essential, active and negative names and any reverential wording in one's capacity, citing 2:286. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows conventional attribute or act names except figurative or defect-suggesting ones. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī sees no exegetical restriction but advises caution in formal naming."}, {"id": "7:180/q17/p3", "position": "A truthful attribute may be predicated even where a new name may not be given.", "reasons": "Al-Ghazālī says descriptions make truth claims, while names require a rightful namer. Al-Ālūsī replies that implication may still bar a predicate; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī treats ordinary predication as freer than formal naming."}, {"id": "7:180/q17/p4", "position": "God should not be invoked as 'thing' or by other abstract terms lacking reverent sanction.", "reasons": "Jahm says 'thing' applies even to base or nonexistent things, argues from 42:11 and creation verses, and notes no devotional precedent. {"id": "7:180/q25", "question": "Who deviates in God's names, and how?", "turns_on": "Whether this is idol-naming, unauthorized descriptions, denial, shirk, or spiritual abuse; some sources include several forms.", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q25/p1", "position": "Idolaters transfer, alter or derive God's names for idols.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid cite al-Lāt from Allah, al-ʿUzzā from al-ʿAzīz and Manāt from al-Mannān; Maqātil adds Hubal, Asaf and Nāʾila. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī adds place, sensory perception, injustice and ignorance. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī lists corporeality, place, sensory perception, humanlike powers, injustice and ignorance as wrongly ascribed defects. Al-Māwardī also reports naming God father of the Messiah and Ezra; al-Rāzī cites Karrāmiyya calling God body and Muʿtazilites saying an act would make Him foolish. Al-Ālūsī discusses hand, face, descent and arrival as scriptural expressions requiring interpretation rather than literal creaturely attribution."}, {"id": "7:180/q25/p3", "position": "They associate partners or assign divine powers and perfections to created things.", "reasons": "Qatāda glosses ilḥād as shirk. Al-Qāshānī says seeking divine attributes elsewhere is deviation; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī lists matter, time, idols, prophets, saints and independent causes. Kuran Yolu includes near-divine flattery of rulers and shaykhs."}, {"id": "7:180/q25/p4", "position": "They deny or reject genuine names, especially al-Raḥmān.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reports denial; al-Kashshāf and al-Bayḍāwī cite opponents accepting only the Raḥmān of Yamāma. Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers this as the immediate point: mockery of several names for one God."}, {"id": "7:180/q25/p5", "position": "They lie or speak falsehood about God's names.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda supply this gloss; some reports pair it with denial. Al-Ṭabarī calls it falsehood."}, {"id": "7:180/q25/p6", "position": "They alter the names or insert what does not belong.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash gives alteration; al-Aʿmash describes insertion into the names, and al-Khaṭṭābī calls erroneous naming ilḥād."}, {"id": "7:180/q25/p7", "position": "Inwardly, it includes failing to embody attributes or claiming a false spiritual station.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī treats failure to embody attributes as deviation. Al-Qushayrī contrasts excess anthropomorphism with deficient negation and lists imagined nearness, hidden evil, falling rank, hypocrisy, grand claims and ingratitude."}, {"id": "7:180/q25/p8", "position": "They distort through imitation or resemblance.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim gives a parallel gloss of ilḥād in signs at 41:40; ʿAṭāʾ gives imitation or resemblance."}, {"id": "7:180/q25/p9", "position": "They turn away from the truth.", "reasons": "Zayd ibn Aslam supplies this explanation."}, {"id": "7:180/q25/p10", "position": "They are thirsty.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī reports ʿAṭāʾ's gloss ẓāmiʾūn without elaboration."}]}
{"id": "7:180/q26", "question": "How does fī in 'fī asmāʾihi' function?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q26/p1", "position": "It can mark cause: they deviate because of or over God's names.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers this construal, comparing a hadith of a woman entering Hell because of a cat and Ibn Abī Rabīʿa's poem about acting because of a beloved."}]}
{"id": "7:180/q27", "question": "What does 'leave those who deviate' instruct?", "turns_on": "Threat, nonconfrontation, or rejection of their practice.", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q27/p1", "position": "Leave them to God's coming punishment and ignore their objections; the command is a threat.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī compares 15:3 and 29:66; al-Qurṭubī compares 74:11 and 15:3, arguing from the recompense clause. Al-Ālūsī says the promise answers why believers can disregard them. Al-Bursawī says avoiding their heresy averts punishment; the warning consoles believers, as al-Ālūsī and Islahi explain."}, {"id": "7:180/q27/p2", "position": "Avoid prolonged debate or confrontation with those uninterested in truth.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd supplies no-debate reading; Ibn ʿĀshūr says their doubts may mislead ordinary believers. Al-Qurṭubī adds exclusive worship and avoidance of deviants."}, {"id": "7:180/q27/p3", "position": "Abandon their misnaming rather than literally abandoning the persons.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī says leaving people themselves makes no sense; the Najmiyya interpretation says deviants are left to nature and desire."}]}
{"id": "7:180/q28", "question": "Was the command to leave them abrogated?", "turns_on": "Whether a no-confrontation order was superseded by fighting or the wording remains a threat.", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q28/p1", "position": "Ibn Zayd says fighting abrogated the order to leave unbelievers without confrontation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn al-Jawzī and Abū Ḥayyān transmit it."}, {"id": "7:180/q28/p2", "position": "The verse remains operative because the command is a threat, not a ban on confrontation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī explicitly rejects abrogation; the majority in Ibn al-Jawzī cite 74:11. Al-Qurṭubī points to the attached recompense."}]}
{"id": "7:180/q29", "question": "When and how will the deviants be recompensed?", "turns_on": "Hereafter alone or also this world.", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q29/p1", "position": "They will be punished in the Hereafter for habitual disbelief, distortion and other deeds.", "reasons": "Maqātil, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya specify the Hereafter. Ibn ʿĀshūr says mā covers all acts of heart and tongue, sa- confirms futurity and kānū yaʿmalūn depicts persistence."}, {"id": "7:180/q29/p2", "position": "Requital may occur in both this world and the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports it; al-Biqāʿī says the passive highlights certainty of punishment rather than its agent."}]}
{"id": "7:180/q30", "question": "How does the recompense clause stress the warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q30/p1", "position": "The recompense clause answers an implied question and marks punishment as certain and repeated conduct as habitual.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes the connective fa; Ibn ʿĀshūr interprets sa- and kānū yaʿmalūn,."}]}
{"id": "7:180/q31", "question": "How does the verse connect with its context and parallels?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q31/p1", "position": "After 7:179's heedlessness and Hell warning, remembrance through the names offers a way away from that fate.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān contrast worldly cravings and darkness with remembrance and obedience; Abū Ḥayyān gives making up missed prayers as example. Al-Ālūsī, Asad and Study Quran link the heedless to this verse."}, {"id": "7:180/q31/p2", "position": "It recalls the innate pledge at 7:172, the humble prayer command at 7:55, and other beautiful-name verses.", "reasons": "Islahi invokes the pledge; al-Biqāʿī cites 7:55. Al-Rāzī lists 17:110, 20:8 and 59:24, also cited by later writers. Kuran Yolu, citing Ibn al-ʿArabī, adds that the names awaken reverence, help prayer, comfort hearts, elevate the reciter, and teach sound belief about what is necessary, possible and impossible for God."}, {"id": "7:180/q31/p3", "position": "The passage interrupts condemnation of polytheists to reaffirm divine oneness and reject their naming errors.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr makes their rejection of Raḥmān the context; al-Biqāʿī says perfect names forestall blaming God for misguidance and lead to the group at 7:181. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī contrasts worship through the names with their distortion. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī adds that misguidance is privative but persists when God withholds success through respite and gradual enticement."}, {"id": "7:180/q31/p4", "position": "A related interpretive application extends requital to righteous recipients of revelation across communities.", "reasons": "Asad connects it to Moses' people in 7:159."}]}
